tweets.text:
A list of stats from the Anthropic S-1:

- NDR is ~900%

- Revenue per employee is over $6.6M, up from about $1.4M a year earlier

- Revenue went from $41M three years ago to $16.3B in the first six months of 2026

- Quarterly revenue went from $4.7B in Q1 to $11.6B in Q2

- Q2 2026 was the first profitable quarter: $974M in operating income ($1.7B operating loss the quarter before)

- Adjusted operating income was $1.6B in the first half of 2026, up from a $1.8B adjusted loss a year earlier

- Revenue grew 1,368% year over year in Q2, while compute and infrastructure costs grew 300%

- Compute went from 251% of revenue to 48% in five quarters

- The value of Anthropic’s own internal Claude usage grew 250x from January to September 2026

- Anthropic spends more on tokens (at list price) than on payroll

- Over 1,900 customers pay $1M+ a year, and about 250 pay $10M+

- Customers paying $100K+ went from 950 to over 11,900 in a year

- Over half of the Fortune 500 pays $100K+ a year

- Those Fortune 500 customers still spend less than 0.1% of their total expenses with Anthropic

- The top 5% of Claude Code users spend roughly 20x what non-users on Claude Enterprise do

- About 40 million smaller customers

- $72.4B of the $80.7B first-half net loss is an accounting charge on convertible notes (not operating losses) 

- Nearly $800B in compute commitments over 10 years
$141.1B raised in total, with over $130B in cash and short-term investments

- Nearly half of revenue comes through Amazon, Google and Microsoft’s cloud marketplaces, all of which also compete with Claude

- A single share held by the seven co-founders carries 50.1% of the vote

- That share is redeemed for nothing if fewer than three founders remain

One of the best tells that a technology will change the world: it makes a chaotic entrance.

In the 1980s, employees lied on procurement forms to get PCs into the office, claiming they were buying oscilloscopes or typewriters, while experts warned of "shadow" data processing departments.

Spreadsheets, the original "workplace agent," filled companies with models only their creator could understand.

Email broke the mailroom's control over who could reach whom.

Each time, the fix was a habitat: guardrails that kept the bottom-up energy alive while reining in the chaos just enough.

Now agents are following the same path. As Replit's Amjad Masad puts it, "Today, most agents live somewhere chaotic. They run in chat windows, personal accounts, and one-off scripts, holding whatever credentials and data someone handed them."

"Code is the ultimate 'aligning artifact' that someone can produce, because it literally is the business logic of the organization."

"Soon, you'll be able to measure a company's alignment by the richness of its agent habitat."

Marc Andreessen on Replit and the dawn of the self-driving company: https://t.co/MnDCH9X0vi

@Replit @amasad

OpenAI's computer-using agents can now operate almost any app the way a person does, clicking and typing through software that never got an API, and the team building them says they're close to beating expert humans on speed.

Ari Weinstein works on OpenAI's consumer computer use products, and James Sun works on the enterprise side. Both were startup founders before joining OpenAI.

Some time ago, I came across research from ETH Zürich showing that 27% of 108,667 large Ethereum swaps were executed at suboptimal prices.

Researchers analyzed swaps over $30K and found that better routing could have saved nearly 30,000 trades at least $30.

Here are 5 things I learned ↓

1️⃣ A direct swap doesn't always give you the most tokens

Let's say you're swapping $ETH for $USDC.

You have several options:

• Swap directly through an ETH/USDC pool
• Route through ETH → USDT → USDC
• Split your order across several liquidity pools

Each option has different liquidity, price impact, and gas costs.

The ETH Zürich study found that optimizable trades could have received an average of 0.15% more through better routing.

For a $100,000 swap, that's an extra $150. This is exactly why DEX routers exist.

Fynd, for example, is the router @PropellerSwap built to find the best swap routes across liquidity pools.

But finding the best route is only half the problem.

2️⃣ Your swap route can become outdated before it executes

Here's something most DeFi users don't realize.

When you request a swap, the router calculates a route based on current liquidity and prices. You approve the tx, sign it, and wait for it to execute onchain.

That process can take a fraction of a second or stretch into tens of seconds.

During that time:

• Another trader can move prices in your chosen pool
• Liquidity providers can withdraw funds
• Arbitrageurs can eliminate price differences
• Market makers can update their quotes

So the route that looked optimal when you signed might be significantly worse when your transaction actually executes.

A perfectly calculated quote can become outdated within milliseconds.

3️⃣ Integrated route optimization

This was the most interesting part of my research.

Most traditional routers calculate execution paths before transactions are submitted, and some prepare alternative routes or fallback options in case conditions change.

These approaches still have limitations, and newer alternatives are emerging:

Fynd InBlock is one of them. Instead of relying on routes calculated beforehand, it lets block builders run an entirely new route search immediately before the tx executes.

• You submit a swap with an initial route
• The block builder processes preceding transactions
• Fynd, running inside the block builder, searches for a better route using the updated pool states
• If a better route exists, it can replace the original

It's essentially performing a fresh search based on the liquidity available at your exact position inside the block.

4️⃣ What if there's no optimal route?

Imagine swapping $50,000 in $ETH for $USDC.

Your original route uses Pool A, but another trader moves its price before your transaction executes.

Pool B now offers a better deal.

Instead of sticking with the outdated route, Fynd InBlock can discover Pool B and switch before execution.

If no better route exists, your trade uses the original route, subject to the same minimum output requirement.

5️⃣ Beyond DEX aggregators

Better execution benefits the entire trading infrastructure:

• Wallets can offer more reliable swaps
• Trading terminals can reduce failed transactions and slippage
• Aggregators can compete on actual execution quality
• Block builders can earn revenue from improving routes

The ETH Zürich research showed how much value inefficient routing leaves on the table.

My prediction is that the next moat in DEX execution isn't finding the best route faster, but rather finding the best route at the exact moment your trade executes.

If you want to read more about how Fynd InBlock works, start here:
https://t.co/aZcClI5kuh

• Market makers can update their quotes

So the route that looked optimal when you signed might be significantly worse when your transaction actually executes.

A perfectly calculated quote can become outdated within milliseconds.

3️⃣ Integrated route optimization

This was the most interesting part of my research.

Most traditional routers calculate execution paths before transactions are submitted, and some prepare alternative routes or fallback options in case conditions change.

These approaches still have limitations, and newer alternatives are emerging:

Fynd InBlock is one of them. Instead of relying on routes calculated beforehand, it lets block builders run an entirely new route search immediately before the tx executes.

• You submit a swap with an initial route
• The block builder processes preceding transactions
• Fynd, running inside the block builder, searches for a better route using the updated pool states
• If a better route exists, it can replace the original

It's essentially performing a fresh search based on the liquidity available at your exact position inside the block.

4️⃣ What if there's no optimal route?

Imagine swapping $50,000 in $ETH for $USDC.

Your original route uses Pool A, but another trader moves its price before your transaction executes.

Pool B now offers a better deal.

Instead of sticking with the outdated route, Fynd InBlock can discover Pool B and switch before execution.

Better execution benefits the entire trading infrastructure:

• Wallets can offer more reliable swaps
• Trading terminals can reduce failed transactions and slippage
• Aggregators can compete on actual execution quality
• Block builders can earn revenue from improving routes

The ETH Zürich research showed how much value inefficient routing leaves on the table.

My prediction is that the next moat in DEX execution isn't finding the best route faster, but rather finding the best route at the exact moment your trade executes.

tweets.text:
Anthropic is a very impressive business - a few charts after having ai run through the S-1. Not much of a single stocks guy and a thousand smarter analysts pouring over this rn than me but my surface level take is it’s a very strong business. 

In terms of the future outlook, feels like the key risk here is the sustainability for frontier models to sell tokens at a high margin or whether it gets commoditized down as use case needs for the average person begin to reach an asymptote where the marginal new frontier model doesn’t change the quality of experience and output for the average task. 

There will always be a need for frontier tokens by a certain subset of users but feels to me like the question is whether the average Fortune 500 company prefers a frontier token vs the commoditized one. 

There’s also the dynamic around data privacy. How willing will companies be to fork over their company info into training data vs build their own model trained on open weight models. 

On net, the company seems highly sustainable short term and liquidity ratios are very solid, but the outlook on demand for premium high margin tokens is the key question.

That’s why people are disappointed. PMs were meant to suck in data that would beat the polls.

tweets.text:
I've been doing a lot of my token research with AI agents lately.

I started out giving pretty explicit instructions about what to dig into, but now I can literally say "do a deep dive on [XYZ]" and it'll go off and do some insane research cause it knows what I want

If you want to get your AI thinking along the same lines, here's a bunch of the things I initially asked for:

1. Explain what [XYZ] does and how its best users actually use it, in plain English.

2. Show me fees paid by real users (last 30 and 90 days annualised vs the last 12 months), and how much is just incentives or points farming.

3. Who owns the supply, when are the unlocks, and what have the team and investors sold? Check onchain where you can, because CoinGecko is often out of date.

4. Compare it to its closest competitors on FDV and revenue.

5. Make the bear case as strong as you can, with the best reply to each point.

6. Source and date every number. If you can't find something, say so. Don't guess.

7. Finish with rough bear, base and bull odds and a price for each.

Still absolutely blows my mind how much better Opus 5.5 is compared to anything I used 6 months ago

tweets.text:
🗡️ What DeFi Shipped 🚢 (Oct 26)

Solana now finalizes in about 150ms, Balaji's Network School bought Farcaster, and Privacy Pools shipped a big v2:

9 updates worth catching up on:

• @solana switched on Alpenglow on mainnet, its biggest consensus change since launch. Finality drops from 12.8 seconds to about 150ms.

• Balaji's Network School is buying @farcaster_xyz from @neynarxyz, less than 9 months after Neynar bought it. Farcaster becomes the "Network State Protocol."

• @Ledger launched Agent Intent in beta. AI agents can propose trades and moves, but nothing goes through until you approve it on your Ledger.

Interesting idea but think ledger has had a lot of reputational hits lately.

• @0xprivacypools launched v2 on 7 chains. You can send private payments, request money with a link, earn Aave yield, and swap without leaving the pool. Deposits are still screened, so it stays compliant.

• @Pumpfun partnered with @PreStocks. You can trade pre-IPO tokens for OpenAI, Anthropic, Anduril, Neuralink, Kalshi, Polymarket, and more (not open to US users).

• @defillama launched prediction markets that settle on DefiLlama data, built with @Trueo_'s permissionless markets.

• @Kintsu opened a private beta on @CantonNetwork for lending and staking. Testers can supply USDC, borrow against Canton Coin, and stake CC.

• @longdotxyz turned on community basket management for AINX. Holders now vote on what goes in the basket every 7 days and earn fees from AINX trading.

• @papertrade_xyz says PAPER will stay non-transferable for now. If outside perp markets listed PAPER, attackers could short it while trying to drain the bankroll.

The markets are down but DeFi keeps shipping

Anthropic is now generating ~$2 of revenue for every $1 of compute spend - up from just $0.40 a year ago.

This is a 5x improvement in compute efficiency and clear evidence that AI demand is being monetised at the model layer.

But it doesn’t automatically solve the ROI question for the infrastructure stack. Model companies are customers of the compute; hyperscalers and neoclouds are the ones that have to earn a return on the GPUs, power and data centers after depreciation and financing costs.

The market is currently focused on the cash-flow gap and higher cost of capital. The efficiency gains and sold-out capacity suggest the longer-term demand thesis is still intact.

We continue to see selective opportunities in the highest-quality AI enablers. https://t.co/YKr5pL78cE

tweets.text:
France has the highest government spending to GDP of the major developed countries.

But total spending to GDP is just one measure of the government's impact on the economy, which, at increasingly high levels, is negative.

It's important to look at all three: government spending to GDP, the deficit to GDP, and total debt to GDP.

Spending tells you the raw size of government outlays. The deficit shows whether that spending is funded by taxes or borrowing. Total debt tells you the accumulated deficits.

All three follow the same general finding in economics. A little is necessary. A little more is generally good. But there's a point where the benefits level off. Eventually, the improvement in the standard of living flatlines and then turns negative.

Taken together, France is the worst of the developed countries, but the United States is not far behind. The US actually runs a bigger deficit. Of course, one important difference is the reserve currency, but this speaks more to capacity vs negative impact of increasing government size.

Looking at all three also exposes the inflation fallacy. Inflation can reduce debt to GDP, but with most government spending indexed to inflation, the deficit and spending to GDP don't improve, and those carry consequences too.

As the deficit gets bigger, government borrowing crowds out other borrowers. Many point to AI funding getting crowded out, but I think the impact is downstream. If AI is productive and generates returns, it will keep getting funded, and other sectors get crowded out instead.

Housing is the most obvious example. Housing investment has been weak for 4 years, and the recent rise in interest rates will likely make that worse.

France is currently the most extreme case, but many developed nations are in a similar position, with a level of government size and command-and-control effects on the economy that negatively impact the standard of living.

What is the significance of Serbian election? I have been asked this by a lot of folks, so here is an unusually long post from me. 

The significance is... 

1. ...That this happened before…

2. ...That you have no idea that it happened before…

3. ...And that the West messed it up the first time too.

I am not an expert on Serbian politics. If you want to follow an actual legitimate expert, please follow Professor Dusan Pavlovic (@d_pavlovic) for proper analysis or my elementary school buddy Dimitrije Vojnov (@timjohnbyford) if you want the more anarcho-Hollywood commentary.

Nonetheless, I was born in Belgrade, I left at 13 years old, and am a geopolitical/investment strategist by trade (basketball coach at heart). As such, lots of folks are asking me what is going on in Serbia and what I think about it.

Well, here is what is going on… Serbia has yet again illustrated that it has the capacity for non-violent regime change. Incumbent leader Aleksandar Vucic conceded in a short and relatively sweet manner and the collective will of student protesters won. Pretty extraordinary outcome in today's jaded world. 

If this sounds vaguely familiar to you, it is because it also happened exactly 26 years ago, back in October 2000. Then, student protest movement OTPOR –  in part led by dear friend @SrdjaPopovic – managed to do the unthinkable: use non-violent protest to topple the Slobodan Milosevic regime. The degree of difficulty then was higher than today. Say what you will about Vucic, but his government was not autocratic or engaged in military adventurism. 

But I don’t really want to talk about what happened in Serbia. I want to talk about how the West reacted to the extraordinary defeat of Milosevic in 2000 by a group of pro-West students. 

Instead of embracing the new government, it sought to force it into compliance with a deluge of conditionality. Sure, the incoming Prime Minister Vojislav Kostunica was not aligned with Western liberal values, but this is Serbia 26 years ago! Did Belgrade get a pass after it just toppled, peacefully, the so-called "Butcher of Balkans?" No. It got criticized for everything from LGBTQ+ policy to foreign policy towards Moscow. As if the country was supposed to transition from Serbia to Vermont overnight! It was all sticks all the time, very few carrots for the war-weary country. 

The West then wrestled ~12% of Serbia’s territory – today’s Kosovo – without any real sweeteners and called the Belgrade government obstructionist for opposing it. I don’t want to get into debates of legality or normative justification for Kosovo independence. I think we can all simply agree that giving up ~12% of one’s territory is not an act most countries accept without some sort of constrenation. The US and the EU did not care. They gave Belgrade a fait accompli in a magnificent display of hegemonic arrogance. But hey, it was 2008... different world. 

Underpinning this attitude has long been a general sense of antagonism by the liberal West towards conservative Serbia. In the mind of many foreign policy elites - a generation of elite "experts" for whom the first taste of geopolitics came from the wars in Yugoslavia - Serbia and Serbs are and always will be the "bad guys." Belgrade, effectively, has had to pay the price for the 1990s, even once the regime that underwrote that aggressive policy of that terrible decade was peacefully and extraordinarily toppled in 2000. The incredible enthusiasm and pro-West sentiment of that youth - the youth that stared Milosevic regime right in the face with no fear - was ignored and wasted. Many of that youth is no longer pro-EU or pro-West. It is jaded, nihilist, and very bitter. 

I can see the same outcome on the horizon for Serbia today. The West is going to expect instant compliance, but 60% of Serbs do not want an antagonistic relationship with Russia. As such, expecting these students today to just throw away the country's relationship with Moscow is naive. Public support for accession to the EU is as low as 32%, according to some surveys, as high as a pathetic 45% in others. That is extremely low for a country that would objectively benefit from EU membership. The West’s brand has lost its luster. 

If the West wants Serbia to actually change its geopolitical direction, it’s going to have to pay for that shift. No, Serbia will again not become Vermont overnight. It won’t be a bastion of liberal thought or values. So what? Judging by election results in the West, doesn’t seem like this should be a problem, now should it? The West appears to have approximated Serbia over the past quarter century. So, all should be good, no?

Serbia is also not going to give up its relationship with the Global South. Not unless Europeans and Americans pay for the shift. This is a multipolar world folks. If Belgrade stood by its geopolitical independence at the very height of American hegemony, the price for its compliance just went up, not down. You had your chance to "buy" Serbia cheap in 2000. If the students protesting in the streets of Belgrade listened to their game theory lessons, they should play hard-to-get this time around. 

What the reaction in the West should be – and should have been in 2000 – is to celebrate the example that Serbian students just set. French students should, especially, get to studying the example set by the Serbs. As should young people in the Global South, India and elsewhere. This kind of change takes hard work, concentration, and an iron will commitment to non-violence. Now two generations of Serbian students – the generation from the 1990s and now this one 25 years later – have shown the world how to do peaceful change. 

The question is not whether Serbs learned any lessons, but whether the West did. If the West actually cares which way Serbia leans – and it is not clear to me that it actually does – then it is going to have to stop trying to fight its own domestic ideological battles inside Serbian society. You want Belgrade to join the West? Then stop lecturing and start paying.

alright, anthropic s-1 is way more optimistic than i expected, the numbers tell me they're playing at the big boy table, my bull/bear takeaway:

- anthropic has a probable path to profitability: revenue is impressive but the efficiency of that revenue is what matters, $1 of compute invested now gives you $2.08 of rev.

- 900% NRR is absolutely insane. a company spending $1M at the start of the year ends up spending $9M by end of year which means claude models really ARE that good vs. competition.

- cash balance is fantastic: $132 billion which puts them on the same playing field as Meta, google and other hyperscaler spending. anthropics at the big boy table.

- claude cowork and opus 5.5 are killing it with token consumption up-only. this dispels the narrative that openai and open source is coming for their throne.

the bear case:

- VERY heavy capex spending with $120B going to one of their big competitors that could cut them off i.e. spaceX. elon has become the toll-collector for compute

- future rev is expected to slow down as we have a period of consolidation. solving things like cancer and stuff (while amazing) will take time.

- anthropic's success is contingent on achieving RSI. i personally think this is achievable in the next 6-9 months but who knows.

bring on the IPO!

People will tell you that beating the S&P 500 is hard. But is simple, not necessarily easy, but simple. 

After over 30 years of trading, here is what I've learned.

First, my Duke MBA is +/- worthless for trading, but does help me understand jargon and fundamentals, so not a total waste.

Second, it is like poker. The key is folding most of the time and only betting when your turn comes around.

Third, most years, it's only 2-4 / year that you should place trades/allocate capital. This is the key. You do NOT buy and sell and every week, every day or even every month.

Fourth, and this more art than science, you just wait for some narrative to get so ridiculous in one direction that you have to wade in for the reverse.

Fifth, do not think you will time the bottom or the top. I like to buy low and then buy lower and then buy higher. 

Examples this year, which I posted on as times to buy. Let me repeat this again, everything I mentioned below as a time to buy is recorded on my X feed.

First, I said to buy software during the SaaS breakdown. At around 80 on the IGV, I was a buyer, now over 110, almost a 40% gain.

Second, I said to buy a basket of AMZN, GOOG, MSFT, and META in June at a price of 1335. It went to 1939 in a couple months, a 45% gain.

Third, I said to buy bonds a month ago when the the 10 year was at 5.3%.

A week or so ago, I said to buy semis, buy the SOXX. I also think buying Brazil, EWZ, is the play now.

Those two last picks above might look stupid a week or two from now. But just wait. 

In 5-6 months, I will repost this with the SOXX and EWZ performance since this post. My guess, a 30-50% gain easy.

Stop with the one-day options, the leverage, the 3x ETFs and all the bullshit.

Stop with being smart and analyzing all the trends and looking perfect.

Buy low. Then buy lower, then buy higher, but only of the things that almost must come back. 

You will kill every hedgie on the street. I do.

Crypto has been down this month, yet something beneath it looks different. Applications may finally deserve attention as viable investments.

For spot buyers, without the pre-TGE terms given to insiders and VCs, apps have been a diabolical trade. The average scored app lost 84% in 2022 then lagged smart-contract platforms in the bull market. Liquidity gathered around Bitcoin first, then Ethereum and larger platforms. A useful DeFi product was no guarantee of a rewarding token. Even if a value-accrual mechanism existed, the market didn't seem to care. Unlocks, cyclical casino demand and regulatory hostility undermined the investment case at every turn. 

Now the old financial system needs new rails. The GENIUS Act and a more constructive SEC/CFTC approach give exchanges, banks, asset managers and lenders reason to explore on-chain markets. I see an open financial system taking shape, with new businesses run by code. Some applications are becoming serious businesses, with real revenues, operating metrics that outshine legacy firms, and I finally see capital discipline in parts of the sector.

Since March 2025, the top third of scored apps on my Quality screen gained 64.8% net while the average lost 10.6%. That is hard to ignore. But it's < 2 years of data in a 5-year backtest, not live proof of alpha; over the full period since 2022, the top third trails the average. We need to follow it live.

Ar @RealVision, I am integrating a new Helios Analytics dashboard for Alpha and Pro members this week. I think it will be essential for understanding what sits behind a token, alongside adoption, valuation, technicals and liquidity. 

If you haven't already, join us here https://t.co/oApcjkVLeY

$XRP
$XLM
$HBAR
$SUI

Whenever they get a meaningful squeeze, you can bonk them

The dino coins had an insane run in late 2024, and then pumped strongly again during the next risk-on season in mid 2025, which is quite rare, and implies that the digestion/under-performance phase will be very long. TRUMP is now a worthless memecoin that is programmed to fade into irrelevance. Here, the only thing that matters is to avoid being a victim of the short squeezes such as the one we had in August (impressive +160% pump). But TRUMP will trade below $1 at some point, and once again, shorting the squeezes is a gift.

Anthropic's S-1 is 300+ pages so I turned it into a video that focuses on the basics but also hidden facts.

Some interesting things it found:
• The $80.7B "loss" is ~$81B of non-cash marks on convertible notes. Operations lost just $0.7B
• One share holds 50.1% of the vote. Amazon and Google own huge stakes with zero votes
• At a $2T valuation, each co-founder is worth ~$28B, and they pledged 80% of it to charity
• The Pentagon labeled Anthropic a "supply-chain risk" after it refused surveillance and autonomous-weapons uses. Anthropic lost 2–1 on appeal
• 80%+ of revenue comes from models less than 6 months old
• Broadcom's $42B financing jumps from 9% to 13% interest if growth slips
• ~40 million customers sit below the $100K tier

ANTHROPIC'S IPO DOCUMENTS ARE CALMING DOWN THE MARKETS.

None of the numbers released today are that different from what we heard last week, but now we know how much cash they have. 

Anthropic has $120B in cash and is likely raising $100B on the IPO. They are then likely going to be raising another $100B in debt, $60B of it already financed by BlackStone. If you assume a 3x in ARR, which probably is low considering how much the street wants them to grow, this company should have around $300-$400B in cash. This also doesn't take into account the future ATMs they might engage in.

So, the reason AI stocks are getting some relief right now is because it seems like Anthropic will have enough cash to pay their bills, which obviously is good for $NVDA, $SPCX, $AMD, $AVGO, $MU, and many other players. 

However, there are going to be 24 separate unlocks in 2027. Those are going to be days where the market has to deal with a massive amount of supply coming onto the market. The company effectively has unilateral control, not shareholders, on deciding to pause or slow down the release of models. The open-weight models continue to be a threat as more enterprises are seeing the value in owning their AI for a significantly cheaper cost. Anthropic has outlined all these risks in the S1.

Regardless on if you are buying the IPO, it seems like there is enough cash they can raise to continue paying their bills and making sure the downstream value flows into most of the semis...if the market changes their mind on that or Anthropic stalls in growth, those names get hit. But if the company keeps growing and raises cash, the money should be there to fund the semis...it's now a question on how much of a risk people want to take in actually owning the stock.

tweets.text:
My quick takeaways on the Anthropic S-1:

1. This is a historical moment 

2. $6.6M in revenue per employee!! Hard to even comprehend how good that is but Anthropic is AI native as it gets so makes sense. 

3. I always thought OpenAI would drop their S-1 first 

4. Customers spend about 9x more after a year. Net Revenue Retention is approximately 900% as of Sep 30, 2026. Good SaaS companies brag about 120%.

5. Cowork is growing faster than Claude Code did. Goes to show you the demand for consumer products. Duo will probably rip.

6. 3 years ago this company did $41M in revenue. In the first six months of 2026, it did $16.3 billion. I don't think anyone has a mental model for that curve yet, I sure don’t. 

7. Nearly half of revenue comes through cloud marketplaces. About 48% comes from customers buying through them. Big companies buy where their budget already lives, and the lesson for founders selling to enterprises is to get listed where your buyers already spend.

8. Their run rate formula is published: the last 28 days of usage times 13, plus subscriptions times 12, which i guess is the new ARR math for founders?

9. It looks like They're merging Cowork into Claude dot au which tells you the chat box era is ending and the "go do the work for me" era is here.

10. Thousands of Anthropic employees are about to become liquid at once, so expect the biggest wave of new AI startups and angel checks San Francisco has ever seen. Reminds me when Facebook went public but this is way bigger. 

Let’s go! 

11. Buried in the filing, Anthropic says the gap between what Claude can do and how widely it's used is one of its biggest growth opportunities, so the company itself is telling you the models are ahead of the market and someone has to close that gap for dentists, landlords, and plumbers.

12. Whatever happens, exciting times to be building in AI.

$META

META OFFICIALLY ENTERS THE CAPITAL RAISING GAME THROUGH SELLING MORE OF THEIR STOCK.

Meta announced plans to raise approximately $35 billion through two equity offerings:

- $22.5B in Class A common stock through forward sale agreements.

- $12.5B in depositary shares tied to mandatory convertible preferred stock.

The company is also considering a separate $60 billion offering program for its new nonvoting Class C shares, potentially beginning in Q1 2027. The nonvoting class was introduced on earnings last week and will result in a 2-for-1 stock split. 

The total raise so far will be around $95B, $10B more than Google’s $85B equity offering from a few months ago. 

$NVDA NVIDIA, $AMD, and $AVGO Broadcom have also expressed nonbinding interest in purchasing a combined $5 billion of Meta shares…which basically means the suppliers of chips to Meta will now be taking a direct equity stake into them. Meta already has warrants that convert into shares for 10% of $AMD if it holds above $600 in the future. 

Capital is now becoming the constraint…whoever can raise the most will win.

$META

META OFFICIALLY ENTERS THE CAPITAL RAISING GAME THROUGH SELLING MORE OF THEIR STOCK.

Meta announced plans to raise approximately $35 billion through two equity offerings:

- $22.5B in Class A common stock through forward sale agreements.

- $12.5B in depositary shares tied to mandatory convertible preferred stock.

The company is also considering a separate $60 billion offering program for its new nonvoting Class C shares, potentially beginning in Q1 2027. The nonvoting class was introduced on earnings last week and will result in a 2-for-1 stock split. 

The total raise so far will be around $95B, $10B more than Google’s $85B equity offering from a few months ago. 

$NVDA NVIDIA, $AMD, and $AVGO Broadcom have also expressed nonbinding interest in purchasing a combined $5 billion of Meta shares…which basically means the suppliers of chips to Meta will now be taking a direct equity stake into them. Meta already has warrants that convert into shares for 10% of $AMD if it holds above $600 in the future. 

Capital is now becoming the constraint…whoever can raise the most will win.
